en: The Kauhalīya Śikṣā:
Now I shall proclaim the Śikṣā following the doctrine of Kauhalīya; therein the determination of vowels and other elements is made—listen to that! 1.
The acute (udātta), the grave (anudātta), the circumflex (svarita), and likewise the protracted (pracaya)—
thus have four accents been declared by the wise. That which is uttered with high pitch is designated as the acute (udātta).
The wise specifically state that extension, firmness, and subtlety in the limbs and likewise in the throat produce the acute (udātta) accent. That which is uttered low is called the grave (anudātta).
They know that *prasrta* (flowing) causes softness and bulkiness of the limbs and so forth.
*Svarita* is declared in the case of lowness (*nīcatva*), and it is desired in the junction of those two;
they know the first half of that *svarita* to be higher-pitched.
The remaining half is considered to be very low-pitched because it is slight;
some know its first portion to be similar to udātta,
while the remainder is equal to anudātta— thus they are remembered as being twofold.
The *pracaya* (accumulated accent) is described by the wise as having an auditory quality similar to the *udātta*.
The seven types of *svarita* should be known; they will be explained in detail:
the *nitya*, the *kṣaipra*, the *abhinihata*, the *praśliṣṭa*, and likewise the *prātihata*.
Likewise, there is the *pādavṛtta*, as well as the *tairovyañjana-svarita*.
Some call it *aṇumātraka*, while others describe it as a different kind of accent (*svaramanya*).
That which follows an acute (*udātta*) and is lower in pitch at the junction [of sounds] is known as the *svarita*.
If it is followed by a word-accented (svāra-udātta) syllable, then this [svarita] is considered to be depressed (nihata); however, they consider its cognition to be natural (prākṛta).
When a low-pitched (nīca) syllable follows a svarita at a junction, it is considered a continuous (pracaya) accent.
Furthermore, when there is plurality, they may likewise be so; however, it is not the case that a *svāra* [svarita] vowel is followed by an acute (*udātta*) one.

In the euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*) of the vowels *i* and *u*, when they become *y* and *v* respectively and are both acute, that which is pronounced as a svarita there is illustrated as this *kṣaipra*.

That which remains unmodified is indeed designated as "eternal" (nitya). When the vowel *o* is acute (*udātta*) and the vowel *e* occurs at the end of a word, that which is circumflex (*svarita*) in their combination through the process of *nihata* with the following vowel [is eternal].
This is called the *abhinihata* accent by the wise.
When a single [vowel] is preceded by an *udātta*, it is always termed *pratihata*.
In the junction of two *ūkāra*s, when followed by an *udātta*, they occur in succession.
In that regard, that which is uttered with a high pitch (*svarita*) and is closely joined (*praśliṣṭa*) is called *svāra*.
Alternatively, the third or fourth part of it is said to be depressed (*nihata*). The *svāra* which occurs in the separation (*vivṛtti*) of a word is designated as *pādavṛtta*.
Among the *kampa* [melodies], the first is considered to consist of a single atom (*aṇumātrika*).
If there is a conjunction of three of these at their beginning with one another, then the second half of the first is prescribed to be suppressed. 18

The third or fourth part [of the vowel] is considered struck when there is a conjunction (*saṃyoga*) with a *praśliṣṭa* sound, provided it is with one of those [nasals]. Regarding that as well, some authorities accept *kampa* (tremor) in cases of spontaneous pronunciation according to their own preference.
That which is short should be performed as if it were long, because of the drawing out of the short vowel therein (20).
Now, in the section concerning Svāyambhuva, certain *kampas* have been illustrated;
among them, the *udātta* [notes] should be employed, while the suppressed portions (*nihataṃśa*) are as before (21).
For in this context, a short tremor (*hrasva-kampa*) is prescribed for the words "vīryaṃ balaṃ" (vīryaṃ balam iti),
while a long tremor (*dīrgha-kampa*) is enjoined for "tanvāṃ svāyām" (tanvāṃ svāyām iti) and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "te asmad," some do not recite a tremor.
Some wise men declare that it is contrary to the [established] characteristics;
"Why is this word not struck [as defective]? For what reason would there be its meaninglessness?"—thus various faults are observed by the learned. (23–24)
In this unrefined recitation, however, the *sādhu* (correct) pronunciation of individual phonemes is desired;
yet in the Veda, numerous instances of variation in vowels and consonants are observed.
These are called *vikramas*, and they should be understood by the wise as being of six kinds.
One [svarita] has both [accents], while another has both udātta [accents];
one svarita is preceded by udātta, and yet another exists as being preceded by [an independent] svarita. One is the opposite of this, and likewise, there is that which is preceded by pracaya.
Understand that the *parodātta* is likewise followed by a *svāra*;
however, where a *nihata* is observed between two *svarita*s, this is called *vikrama*, and it is designated as having both *svarita*s. 27–28.
The other steps should be inferred by the wise in this manner; one should exert firm effort while remaining self-controlled in these steps.
There are many that are high-pitched (udātta), low-pitched (anudātta), and also protracted (pluta).
When [svarita] vowels are seen without intervals, there is no combination of them.
Where udātta vowels are seen together without intervals, among those, a progressively higher pitch is prescribed in sequence. 30–31.
They know that for unaccented vowels, there is a levelness; when a circumflex (svarita) vowel occurs in conjunction with a low-pitched (anudātta) one, it is known as even lower than low.
Furthermore, a tremor (kampa) was previously described in the case of a conjunction of circumflex vowels. Having understood these initial steps, one should correctly pronounce the Vedic seer's text.
But that brahmin who especially desires constant spiritual welfare should know the ninefold characteristic of the accents of words:
namely, the circumflex at the end (antodātta), the circumflex at the beginning (ādyudātta), the acute (udātta), and so forth. 33–34.

The middle-acute (madhyodātta), the acute (udātta), the circumflex (svarita), the depressed (nihata), and likewise the single-circumflex (ekasvarita)— these are remembered as the nine sounds of the word.
A wise person should indicate these accents with the right hand.
One seeking great excellence should never [use] the left hand (36).
If that [hand] should prove fruitless for him, those who are wise declare that it is because of his lack of knowledge; therefore, this should be understood by one who knows. (37)
One should indicate the little finger, the ring finger, the middle finger, and the forefinger—held in a low tone (*nīcasvara*) with the tips of the thumbs placed upon them—as the *udātta* accents.
Having placed the gentle *dvisvara* on the middle joint, one should touch it. 38.
In this world he attains fame, and after death he is glorified in heaven.
But that mortal who, deluded in mind, points out otherwise than this, shall go to a terrible hell and be born in sinful wombs. 39–40.

But for that best of Veda-knowers who is habituated to the arrangement of musical notes, whatever merits and defects exist therein through his hand are clearly productive of results; just as for one performing a sacrifice, the Dākṣāyaṇa-sava is the primary means.
Therefore, one who desires abundant welfare should apply oneself to that;
having first studied according to rule from a virtuous Ṛṣi teacher, the wise person must certainly thereafter perform the recitation of the *padas*. 42–43.
Thereafter, one should study the *krama* [recitation], endowed with the correct accents and grammatical refinements;
for in this way, there is constant excellence of attention.
In that [tradition] where the author of the commentary is Ātreya, the *padakrama* belongs to Karṇin.
The wise who know that great branch attain great prosperity.

Having proceeded by steps from both [directions] and having taken back the subsequent [portion] of those two, one should join it with the very next [verse] and complete it at the end of the half-verse.
If one should perform [the recitation] according to its characteristics, without distraction, and in accordance with the proper method,
then first that word [is treated as such], and the subsequent word is like it.
(47) Repetition of an avasāna or a pragraha is not permitted.
Nevertheless, Ātreya maintains that here [the *pluti*] belongs to those two [vowels].

One should recognize as a *trikrama* (three-step) *pluti* that which is seen ending in the vowel *ā*, having an acute accent (*udātta*), and followed by the particle *āṅ*; for example, *moṣūṇaḥ* and *ūṣuṇaḥ*.
In the *trikrama* which is about to be described, first is the *tripadakrama*;
then, because there is no distinction among those [steps] due to the middle and the end, all the steps that have been obtained for it [follow]. 50.
Furthermore, what is the sequence between *suvar*, *karh*, *otar*, *antarā*, *virvi*, and *vaḥ*? [The answer is: "Who awakened? (*ajīgarit*).
This series of words, together with the letter *r*, is the *ājyaptā*.
Thus, one who studies the sequence in this manner becomes free from all defects. 51.

He who desires to speak of the matted locks attains the highest good and reaches the state of divinity; that Brahmin, the most learned in the Vedas, his fame shall increase and he enjoys the fruit of the Vedas. 52-53.

Having proceeded through two words in direct order, then in reverse order, and then in ascending order, one should employ them with proper euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*) and according to their natural phonetic form; that is considered *jaṭā*.
This is declared to be the natural state (*prakṛti*) of the *saṃhitā* of a word, as well as of its sequential arrangement (*krama*).
Understand that this is the nature of the *jaṭā* (matted-hair style) as it is eternally;
when the *jaṭā* is about to be performed, tremors, joints, tones, and so forth must be applied with skillful attention, as has been described therein. 55-56.

He who knows the Prātiśākhya and other technical treatises, is proficient in all the Śikṣās, and is endowed with the power of intellect—he alone is capable of explaining the Jaṭā. When that which has been studied and understood can be expressed merely by recitation (nigada), [then he has truly mastered it]. 57.
Then they entered while not eating; thereafter it blazed for someone.
(58) There are three modes of speech—rapid, medium, and slow—which should be employed with restraint; thus the wise declare regarding the Veda. (59)
If there were a difference between the *vṛttis* [of recitation], there would be a distinction here among the actions;
however, the distinction regarding the *vṛtti* is certainly only slight.
For the purpose of practice, the *vṛtti* should be rapid, but for the purpose of formal performance, it should be moderate.
For the purpose of instructing disciples, one should perform the recitation with a slow tempo (vilambita).

One desiring wisdom should perform the Vedic sequence with a fast tempo (druta), while one desiring the exposition of the Vedas should perform it with a medium tempo (madhyama); however, one desiring heaven should perform it with a slow tempo (vilambita).
If those who are prone to negligence, such as the Asuras and others, go to a miserable rebirth,
then a twice-born man who possesses knowledge will certainly go elsewhere;
thus some who are experts in all the scriptures consider it here.

It has been stated skillfully that the middle [measure] alone should be employed. (64) Who is able to describe with precision the measure of the equalities of vowels and syllables, which set the Vedic meters in motion? (65)
Therefore, the medium mode of recitation (vṛtti) should be employed by those most learned in the Vedas;
for when thus constantly and well-refined, the Veda shines forth.
It should be endowed with rhythmic progression and movement, neither too fast nor too slow.
One should speak with a voice endowed with low, high, and natural tones, remaining steady and even;
the wise consider this to be the characteristic of the *mātrā* (temporal measure) in various specific tasks.
In those very tasks, there is a firm grasp [of the rules].
In this context, wise men illustrate the duration of a *mātrā* through the sounds of the blue jay, the crow, and the peacock, following a sequence of one, two, and three [beats].
Thus do the learned proclaim the various characteristics of the *mātrā*.
In every instance, one who desires his own welfare should awaken himself;
he should always place the Praṇava at the beginning and at the end of the Veda.
That which is not preceded by Oṃ flows away, and that which is not followed by it falls apart.
All the Vedas begin with the Praṇava and rest upon the Praṇava;
therefore, the Praṇava must always be employed at the commencement of the Vedas by the wise.
That which is its one-and-a-half-fold [measure], its sound (nāda), consists of a single mātrā.
Or likewise, two [syllables] may occupy half a *tāsu* (a unit of time).
When situated in the *praṇava*, the letter *sa* should have two *mātrās*.
A vowel has one *mātrā*, or two; a consonant, however, has the measure of an atom (*aṇumātrikam*). 73–74.

At the conclusion of the *kāṇḍas*, *praśnas*, and *anuvākas*, the time [for rest] is prescribed; for the *tantras*, it should be ten, eight, or five *mātrās*, and for the [conclusion of] the *samāsa*, it should be three days,
but there is no rest for the *samāsa* itself.
But in the middle of either a word or a sentence, that which has an unseen purpose is prohibited.
This conjunction of the letter *ra* with a sibilant (*ūṣman*) attains the nature of a vowel,
assuming a form with a common place of articulation.
The letter *ṛ* has an initial portion of one *aṇu*-measure; in the middle is the letter *r*, consisting of half a measure (*ardhamātrika*);

likewise, the final portion consists of one *aṇu*-measure. A division is prescribed in the middle. (78) [This applies] if it stands at the beginning of a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*) or is followed by an *anusvāra*.
Likewise, understand that skillfully at the end of the labial vowels;
when *ya* and *va* are found in the *arya* [meter], one should apply this rule.
Therefore, the sage of this entire scripture is pleased. 79–80.
But he who studies this Śikṣā, which illuminates the true essence of the Veda, attains incomparable fame and merges into the supreme Brahman. 81.
The Kauhalīya-Śikṣā is completed.
